bibl.title: Error correction and improved precision of spike timing in converging cortical networks

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether a pool of cortical neurons can transmit an undistorted message to a target, given that every transmission step adds noise
span.quote: Any signal processing can only induce distortion ( Cover and Thomas, 1991 ). In particular, the propagation of spikes via synaptic transmission can only add noise in the form of lost spikes, added background activity, or spike time jitter, requiring a neuronal mechanism to minimize and compensate for added noise.

span.label: how precise and reliable propagation is possible when most cortical connections are weak and probabilistic
span.quote: Perhaps the simplest mechanism for precise and reliable propagation of spiking signals is 1:1 transmission between a source and a target neuron. Indeed, some neurons generate postsynaptic responses that are sufficiently strong to generate postsynaptic action potentials ( Henze et al., 2002 ; Szegedi et al., 2017 ). In particular, pyramidal cells (PYRs) may connect to neighboring neurons with millivolt-scale unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) ( Cossell et al., 2015 ; Pala and Petersen, 2015 ). However, 1:1 transmission cannot compensate for added noise. Furthermore, cortical spike transmission is typically probabilistic and weak: most unitary EPSPs fail to generate spikes in postsynaptic neurons

span.label: the postsynaptic cell is MORE precise than the cells driving it, and its spike train reconstructs the signal better - error correction across a synapse
span.quote: The brain propagates neuronal signals accurately and rapidly. Nevertheless, whether and how a pool of cortical neurons transmits an undistorted message to a target remains unclear. We apply optogenetic white noise signals to small assemblies of cortical pyramidal cells (PYRs) in freely moving mice. The directly activated PYRs exhibit a spike timing precision of several milliseconds. Instead of losing precision, interneurons driven via synaptic activation exhibit higher precision with respect to the white noise signal. Compared with directly activated PYRs, postsynaptic interneuron spike trains allow better signal reconstruction, demonstrating error correction.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Data-driven modeling shows that nonlinear amplification of coincident spikes can generate error correction and improved precision.

span.label: spike timing precision at the pyramidal-cell-to-interneuron interface
span.quote: To determine the precision and reliability timescale of spike transmission in converging neuronal networks, we focused on the interface between PYRs and inhibitory interneurons (INTs; mostly fast-spiking putative parvalbumin-immunoreactive [PV] cells) in association cortices (parietal cortex and hippocampal region CA1) of freely moving mice.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We apply optogenetic white noise signals to small assemblies of cortical pyramidal cells (PYRs) in freely moving mice.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: supralinear (nonlinear) amplification of coincident presynaptic spikes at the postsynaptic interneuron generates both the error correction and the improved precision
span.quote: Data-driven modeling shows that nonlinear amplification of coincident spikes can generate error correction and improved precision.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the nonlinearity leaves isolated spikes unamplified while multiplying coincident ones, so only spikes that several presynaptic cells emit at nearly the same moment drive the target
span.quote: Thus, in both implementations, isolated spikes were not amplified, whereas coincident spiking yielded supra-linear amplification.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: independent background noise scatters each pyramidal cell's spikes differently, but the subset of spikes that happens to align in time across the pool survives the coincidence-detection step and drives the postsynaptic cell more faithfully than any single element
span.quote: Then, every neuron will spike differently due to the background “noise,” but some spikes of the neurons in the activated pool will occur sufficiently close in time to drive postsynaptic activity more robustly than any of the elements of the pool.

span.label: spikes from different presynaptic cells that happen to coincide are amplified nonlinearly, so the coincidences carry the signal and the independent jitter does not
span.quote: Although expected to saturate when driven by correlated noise ( Zohary et al., 1994 ), linear summation may transmit spikes efficiently ( Reich et al., 2001 ). Indeed, increasing the presynaptic pool size experimentally induced higher precision. However, simple summation of the simultaneously recorded spike trains did not replicate the experimental findings. In contrast, nonlinear summation of coincidence spikes ( Stuart and Häusser, 2001 ) was able to drive postsynaptic spiking more precisely than the driving trains.

span.label: error correction and precision improvement via CD of multiple weak synaptic inputs are PARTICULARLY ADVANTAGEOUS WHEN FAILURE of a synapse or a presynaptic neuron occurs
span.quote: We found that error correction and precision improvement via CD of multiple weak synaptic inputs are particularly advantageous when failure of a synapse or a presynaptic neuron occurs. As a practical example of how error correction may work under natural conditions, the WN signal can be viewed as an analog of external input encoding specific sensory information to a pool of neurons, which also receives other activity. Then, every neuron will spike differently due to the background “noise,” but some spikes of the neurons in the activated pool will occur sufficiently close in time to drive postsynaptic activity more robustly than any of the elements of the pool.

span.label: and the receiving dendrites are equipped for it - those of the interneurons studied support nonlinear summation of coincident inputs
span.quote: We found that neuronal response properties are qualitatively different when neurons are driven directly via photocurrents, compared with synaptic inputs. The direct optogenetic activation is largely somatic, whereas excitatory synaptic activation is largely mediated via synapses on the dendrites. Dendrites of PV cells support nonlinear summation of coincident inputs

span.label: Connections inferred from finite recordings are biased toward strong ones, which favours the rival transmission models over the authors' preferred coincidence-detection model.
span.quote: First, determining connectivity from finite data is necessarily biased toward stronger connections.

span.label: The temporal-coding conclusion assumes the synaptically activated and directly activated interneurons are the same kind of cell, which was not tested in the same cells.
span.quote: Second, the finding that postsynaptic INTs exhibit temporal coding rests upon the assumption that the cells tested during synaptic activation (IDA INTs) and the cells tested during direct optogenetic activation (DA INTs) are identical.

span.label: Transmission between pyramidal cells, the case of greatest interest, was not measured.
span.quote: Third, the properties of spike transmission between PYRs, which are of great interest, remain unknown.

span.label: connectivity estimated from finite data is biased toward strong connections, and strong connections favour the rival transmission models rather than this one
span.quote: There are several limitations that should be emphasized. First, determining connectivity from finite data is necessarily biased toward stronger connections. Strong connections favor the LL and SP models of transmission more than the CD model, in which the effect of as few as two presynaptic spikes is amplified by the nonlinearity.

span.label: the temporal-coding conclusion assumes the synaptically driven and directly driven interneurons are the same cells, verified only at the population level
span.quote: Second, the finding that postsynaptic INTs exhibit temporal coding rests upon the assumption that the cells tested during synaptic activation (IDA INTs) and the cells tested during direct optogenetic activation (DA INTs) are identical. We verified that properties do not differ at the population level, but more work is required to directly test the assumption by synaptic and optogenetic activation of the exact same INTs.

span.label: and the case of greatest interest, transmission between pyramidal cells, was not tested at all
span.quote: Third, the properties of spike transmission between PYRs, which are of great interest, remain unknown. Specifically, the present experiments did not explore the precision and reliability timescale of spike transmission from a presynaptic assembly of PYRs to a postsynaptic target PYR. Based on the present results, we hypothesize that IDA INTs facilitate error correction and precision improvement during the transmission of information from one pool of PYRs to another.

span.label: with the definition of temporal coding stated as one plausible choice among several available metrics
span.quote: One approach is to analyze spike trains from the perspective of a downstream target. Here, we operationally defined temporal coding as a reliability profile that peaks at a timescale shorter than the maximal tested timescale, but in fact, we placed rate/temporal coding on a continuous scale. This approach, which does not depend on any reconstruction filter, is based on a spike distance metric that involves convolving spike trains with kernels of gradually increasing temporal support ( Schreiber et al., 2003 ). Clearly, various kernels and other distance metrics are plausible ( Victor and Purpura, 1996 ; van Rossum, 2001 ).

span.label: the data-processing intuition that any step can only add distortion, imported as the thing to be explained away
span.quote: Any signal processing can only induce distortion ( Cover and Thomas, 1991 ). In particular, the propagation of spikes via synaptic transmission can only add noise in the form of lost spikes, added background activity, or spike time jitter, requiring a neuronal mechanism to minimize and compensate for added noise.

span.label: a spike distance metric that involves convolving spike trains with kernels of gradually increasing temporal support, which does not depend on any reconstruction filter
span.quote: One approach is to analyze spike trains from the perspective of a downstream target. Here, we operationally defined temporal coding as a reliability profile that peaks at a timescale shorter than the maximal tested timescale, but in fact, we placed rate/temporal coding on a continuous scale. This approach, which does not depend on any reconstruction filter, is based on a spike distance metric that involves convolving spike trains with kernels of gradually increasing temporal support ( Schreiber et al., 2003 ). Clearly, various kernels and other distance metrics are plausible ( Victor and Purpura, 1996 ; van Rossum, 2001 ).

span.label: convolution kernels of increasing temporal support, used to place rate and temporal coding on one continuous scale
span.quote: One approach is to analyze spike trains from the perspective of a downstream target. Here, we operationally defined temporal coding as a reliability profile that peaks at a timescale shorter than the maximal tested timescale, but in fact, we placed rate/temporal coding on a continuous scale. This approach, which does not depend on any reconstruction filter, is based on a spike distance metric that involves convolving spike trains with kernels of gradually increasing temporal support ( Schreiber et al., 2003 ). Clearly, various kernels and other distance metrics are plausible ( Victor and Purpura, 1996 ; van Rossum, 2001 ).

span.label: nonlinear summation of coincident inputs, used to explain how the receiving cell can be more precise than its drivers
span.quote: We found that neuronal response properties are qualitatively different when neurons are driven directly via photocurrents, compared with synaptic inputs. The direct optogenetic activation is largely somatic, whereas excitatory synaptic activation is largely mediated via synapses on the dendrites. Dendrites of PV cells support nonlinear summation of coincident inputs

span.label: the recorded presynaptic spike trains simply summed, before trying a nonlinear model
span.quote: Although expected to saturate when driven by correlated noise ( Zohary et al., 1994 ), linear summation may transmit spikes efficiently ( Reich et al., 2001 ). Indeed, increasing the presynaptic pool size experimentally induced higher precision. However, simple summation of the simultaneously recorded spike trains did not replicate the experimental findings. In contrast, nonlinear summation of coincidence spikes ( Stuart and Häusser, 2001 ) was able to drive postsynaptic spiking more precisely than the driving trains.

span.label: the same interneurons driven directly by light instead of through their synapses
span.quote: We found that, compared with DA PYRs, postsynaptic INT spike trains enabled better reconstruction of the WN signal and exhibited higher precision, particularly when more presynaptic PYRs were recruited. Error correction and improved precision were consistent with nonlinear amplification of coincident presynaptic inputs. Furthermore, postsynaptic INTs exhibited temporal coding, whereas DA INTs did not.

span.label: the whole experiment repeated in a second brain region
span.quote: To allow generalization beyond the well-mapped circuits of initial sensory processing, we studied local networks in associative brain regions, the parietal cortex and CA1. We found that some temporal properties of spike generation and transmission are qualitatively similar: DA PYRs exhibited a precision of a few milliseconds, whereas IDA INTs exhibited error correction and improved precision. However, we also observed some differences. First, decoding quality and precision were consistently higher in the neocortex than in CA1. Second, improved precision was consistently higher in the neocortex. Some differences may be due to methodological details (light power, number of activated PYRs), whereas others may be functional (diversity between PYRs, number of presynaptic PYRs). Regardless of the differences, postsynaptic error correction, improved precision, and temporal coding were observed in both brain regions examined, suggesting convergent synaptic transmission as a general mechanism for precise information propagation along the cortical PYR-to-INT interface.

span.label: the size of the recruited presynaptic pool varied experimentally
span.quote: PYR-to-interneuron spike transmission exhibits error correction and improved precision • Interneuron precision is higher when a larger pool of presynaptic PYRs is recruited • Error correction and improved precision are consistent with coincidence detection • Interneurons activated by synaptic transmission act as temporal coders

span.label: A THEORETICAL BOUND STATED, THEN BEATEN: ANY SIGNAL PROCESSING CAN ONLY INDUCE DISTORTION, and the propagation of spikes via synaptic transmission CAN ONLY ADD NOISE - lost spikes, added background, or jitter
span.quote: Any signal processing can only induce distortion ( Cover and Thomas, 1991 ). In particular, the propagation of spikes via synaptic transmission can only add noise in the form of lost spikes, added background activity, or spike time jitter, requiring a neuronal mechanism to minimize and compensate for added noise.

span.label: AND THE POSTSYNAPTIC CELL IS MORE PRECISE THAN THE CELLS DRIVING IT: instead of losing precision, interneurons driven via synaptic activation exhibit HIGHER precision, and their spike trains allow BETTER SIGNAL RECONSTRUCTION - DEMONSTRATING ERROR CORRECTION
span.quote: The brain propagates neuronal signals accurately and rapidly. Nevertheless, whether and how a pool of cortical neurons transmits an undistorted message to a target remains unclear. Instead of losing precision, interneurons driven via synaptic activation exhibit higher precision with respect to the white noise signal. Compared with directly activated PYRs, postsynaptic interneuron spike trains allow better signal reconstruction, demonstrating error correction.

span.label: the bound is not broken but redefined - the SIGNAL is carried by a POOL, and the coincidences among its members survive what any single member's jitter destroys
span.quote: We found that error correction and precision improvement via CD of multiple weak synaptic inputs are particularly advantageous when failure of a synapse or a presynaptic neuron occurs. As a practical example of how error correction may work under natural conditions, the WN signal can be viewed as an analog of external input encoding specific sensory information to a pool of neurons, which also receives other activity. Then, every neuron will spike differently due to the background “noise,” but some spikes of the neurons in the activated pool will occur sufficiently close in time to drive postsynaptic activity more robustly than any of the elements of the pool.

span.label: with the simplest mechanism ruled out first - 1:1 transmission CANNOT COMPENSATE for added noise, and most unitary responses FAIL to generate spikes at all
span.quote: Perhaps the simplest mechanism for precise and reliable propagation of spiking signals is 1:1 transmission between a source and a target neuron. Indeed, some neurons generate postsynaptic responses that are sufficiently strong to generate postsynaptic action potentials ( Henze et al., 2002 ; Szegedi et al., 2017 ). In particular, pyramidal cells (PYRs) may connect to neighboring neurons with millivolt-scale unitary excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) ( Cossell et al., 2015 ; Pala and Petersen, 2015 ). However, 1:1 transmission cannot compensate for added noise. Furthermore, cortical spike transmission is typically probabilistic and weak: most unitary EPSPs fail to generate spikes in postsynaptic neurons

span.label: AND LINEAR SUMMATION RULED OUT BY TRYING IT: simple summation of the simultaneously recorded spike trains DID NOT REPLICATE the experimental findings, where nonlinear summation of coincident spikes drove postsynaptic spiking MORE PRECISELY THAN THE DRIVING TRAINS
span.quote: Although expected to saturate when driven by correlated noise ( Zohary et al., 1994 ), linear summation may transmit spikes efficiently ( Reich et al., 2001 ). Indeed, increasing the presynaptic pool size experimentally induced higher precision. However, simple summation of the simultaneously recorded spike trains did not replicate the experimental findings. In contrast, nonlinear summation of coincidence spikes ( Stuart and Häusser, 2001 ) was able to drive postsynaptic spiking more precisely than the driving trains.

span.label: A LONG-STANDING DEBATE DIAGNOSED AS DEFINITIONAL: whether neurons transmit by rate or temporal codes has been discussed extensively, and MUCH OF THE DEBATE IS ROOTED IN DEFINITIONS - a population code can be based on rates and a single neuron code can be temporal
span.quote: The question of whether neurons transmit information via rate or temporal codes has been discussed extensively ( König et al., 1996 ; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2001 ; Cohen and Kohn, 2011 ), and much of the debate is rooted in definitions. The temporal/rate code differentiation is distinct from the mode by which a population of neurons encodes information: a population code can be based on rates, and a single neuron code can be temporal ( Rieke et al., 1997 ).

span.label: AND THE AUTHORS DECLARE THEIR OWN DEFINITION AS ONE CHOICE AMONG PLAUSIBLE OTHERS: we OPERATIONALLY DEFINED temporal coding as a reliability profile peaking below the maximal timescale, but IN FACT we placed rate and temporal coding ON A CONTINUOUS SCALE - and CLEARLY, VARIOUS KERNELS AND OTHER DISTANCE METRICS ARE PLAUSIBLE
span.quote: One approach is to analyze spike trains from the perspective of a downstream target. Here, we operationally defined temporal coding as a reliability profile that peaks at a timescale shorter than the maximal tested timescale, but in fact, we placed rate/temporal coding on a continuous scale. This approach, which does not depend on any reconstruction filter, is based on a spike distance metric that involves convolving spike trains with kernels of gradually increasing temporal support ( Schreiber et al., 2003 ). Clearly, various kernels and other distance metrics are plausible ( Victor and Purpura, 1996 ; van Rossum, 2001 ).

span.label: with the measure's own artefact stated: when the number of spikes is fixed the reliability profile NECESSARILY increases monotonically, and only nonspecific spikes let it show a local peak - so the signature of temporal coding depends on the presence of noise
span.quote: When the number of spikes is fixed, the reliability profile necessarily increases monotonically. However, in the presence of spikes due to nonspecific inputs, the reliability profile may exhibit a local peak.

span.label: THE STANDARD METHOD'S ANSWER IS ABOUT ITS FIRST SPIKE ONLY: a current pulse attenuates over time, EXPLORES ONLY A SUBSET OF THE RESPONSE SPACE, and is influenced by background spiking - the first spike may be millisecond-precise and ADDITIONAL SPIKES ARE LESS PRECISE
span.quote: A classic approach for quantifying the precision and reliability of spike generation is to apply a current pulse to the tested neuron and measure latency and jitter of the resultant spiking. The response to a pulse attenuates over time, explores only a subset of the response space, and is influenced by background spiking. Indeed, previous work showed that, while the first spike after a current pulse may exhibit millisecond-timescale precision, additional spikes are less precise

span.label: and the widely used intervention is called what it is - current injection is used widely to probe spike generation, BUT IS CLEARLY A NON-PHYSIOLOGICAL INTERVENTION
span.quote: In contrast to intracellular current injection, we applied the WN signals to small groups of adjacent neurons using photocurrents. Current injection is used widely to probe spike generation ( Asanuma et al., 1968 ; Mainen and Seinowski, 1995 ; Bacci and Huguenard, 2006 ; Cossell et al., 2015 ; Pala and Petersen, 2015 ), but is clearly a non-physiological intervention.

span.label: THE ROUTE OF ACTIVATION CHANGES WHAT IS MEASURED: response properties are QUALITATIVELY DIFFERENT when neurons are driven directly by photocurrents rather than by synaptic inputs, because direct activation is largely SOMATIC and synaptic activation largely DENDRITIC
span.quote: We found that neuronal response properties are qualitatively different when neurons are driven directly via photocurrents, compared with synaptic inputs. The direct optogenetic activation is largely somatic, whereas excitatory synaptic activation is largely mediated via synapses on the dendrites. Dendrites of PV cells support nonlinear summation of coincident inputs

span.label: A SELECTION BIAS DECLARED THAT WORKS AGAINST THE PAPER'S OWN CONCLUSION: determining connectivity from finite data is NECESSARILY BIASED TOWARD STRONGER CONNECTIONS, and strong connections favour the RIVAL models more than the coincidence one
span.quote: There are several limitations that should be emphasized. First, determining connectivity from finite data is necessarily biased toward stronger connections. Strong connections favor the LL and SP models of transmission more than the CD model, in which the effect of as few as two presynaptic spikes is amplified by the nonlinearity.

span.label: with an assumption named as an assumption - the temporal-coding finding RESTS UPON THE ASSUMPTION that the synaptically and optically driven cells are identical, verified only at the POPULATION level, and MORE WORK IS REQUIRED to test it directly
span.quote: Second, the finding that postsynaptic INTs exhibit temporal coding rests upon the assumption that the cells tested during synaptic activation (IDA INTs) and the cells tested during direct optogenetic activation (DA INTs) are identical. We verified that properties do not differ at the population level, but more work is required to directly test the assumption by synaptic and optogenetic activation of the exact same INTs.

span.label: AND THE CASE OF GREATEST INTEREST LEFT UNTESTED: the properties of spike transmission between pyramidal cells, WHICH ARE OF GREAT INTEREST, REMAIN UNKNOWN
span.quote: Third, the properties of spike transmission between PYRs, which are of great interest, remain unknown. Specifically, the present experiments did not explore the precision and reliability timescale of spike transmission from a presynaptic assembly of PYRs to a postsynaptic target PYR. Based on the present results, we hypothesize that IDA INTs facilitate error correction and precision improvement during the transmission of information from one pool of PYRs to another.

span.label: TWO REGIONS, WITH THE DIFFERENCES SPLIT INTO METHODOLOGICAL AND FUNCTIONAL: decoding quality and precision were consistently higher in one, and SOME DIFFERENCES MAY BE DUE TO METHODOLOGICAL DETAILS - light power, number of activated cells - WHEREAS OTHERS MAY BE FUNCTIONAL
span.quote: To allow generalization beyond the well-mapped circuits of initial sensory processing, we studied local networks in associative brain regions, the parietal cortex and CA1. Second, improved precision was consistently higher in the neocortex. Some differences may be due to methodological details (light power, number of activated PYRs), whereas others may be functional (diversity between PYRs, number of presynaptic PYRs). Regardless of the differences, postsynaptic error correction, improved precision, and temporal coding were observed in both brain regions examined, suggesting convergent synaptic transmission as a general mechanism for precise information propagation along the cortical PYR-to-INT interface.

span.quote: Using WN signals, we found that spike generation exhibits a precision of 2–4 ms. However, even a 3 ms jitter poses a challenge to stable signal propagation.

span.label: 3.2 [2.4 4] ms — median [IQR] spike-timing precision of directly activated neocortical pyramidal cells with respect to the white-noise input
span.quote: The median [IQR] precision of the DA PYRs was 3.2 [2.4 4] ms ( Figure 2 H).

span.label: 191/229 (84%) — proportion of connected pyramidal-to-interneuron pairs in which the postsynaptic interneuron was more precise than its presynaptic pyramidal cell
span.quote: Furthermore, in 191/229 (84%) of the monosynaptic PYR-to-INT pairs, IDA INT precision was higher than DA PYR precision (p < 0.001, Wilcoxon test; Figure 2 K).

span.label: 12 ms — median reliability timescale of synaptically activated interneurons, versus 102 ms for directly activated interneurons
span.quote: Median DA INT timescales were 102 ms, consistently longer than IDA INT timescales (12 ms; p < 0.001, U test; Figure 5 G).

span.label: 9.4 ms — median reliability timescale of synaptically activated interneurons in hippocampal CA1
span.quote: We found that in CA1, IDA INTs exhibited a median timescale of 9.4 ms, shorter than the DA INT timescale (102 ms; Figures 7 E–7H; p < 0.001, U test).

span.label: 1.02 ms — bias-corrected group delay of information transmission from a pyramidal assembly to a single interneuron
span.quote: After bias correction, the group delay was 1.02 ms (95% confidence limits 0.4–1.44 ms; Figure 6 H).

span.label: 0.015 [0.007 0.033] — median [IQR] spike transmission gain, showing that the connections carrying the precise message are weak
span.quote: While indirect transmission induces an additional delay, relatively weak connections are used (median [IQR] spike transmission gain: 0.015 [0.007 0.033]; p < 0.001, Wilcoxon test; Figure 4 C).

span.label: 8,176 — total single units recorded (6,616 pyramidal, 1,560 interneurons) across neocortex and CA1 in 14 freely moving mice over 162 sessions
span.quote: A total of 8,176 units (6,616 PYR and 1,560 INT) were recorded from neocortex (2,625 PYR, 843 INT) and CA1 (3,991 PYR, 717 INT) of 14 freely-moving mice during 162 sessions.

span.label: 239 DA PYRs and 116 IDA INTs — DA PYRs and IDA INTs that exhibited reliable responses overall
span.quote: Overall, 239 DA PYRs and 116 IDA INTs exhibited reliable responses.

span.label: R 2 = 0.7 — share of group variance in precision accounted for by the set of single-neuron properties considered
span.quote: To identify what determines precision, we considered a host of single-neuron properties that together accounted for most group variance (R 2 = 0.7; Figure S3 ).

span.label: 2–4 ms — the precision of spike generation - the number the transmission step is supposed to make worse and instead improves on
span.quote: Using WN signals, we found that spike generation exhibits a precision of 2–4 ms. However, even a 3 ms jitter poses a challenge to stable signal propagation.
